title: Numerical wave tank: focused wave
text:
Context
Floating offshore wind turbines will be installed where winds are strong and waves are powerful, and a breaking wave can hit their floating column much harder than a regular wave. DIMPACT (2020-2023), a research project led by France Energies Marines, set out to include these loads in the design of floating wind turbines. It combined wave-flume experiments at Ifremer with numerical simulations and produced engineering methods for breaking-wave loads.

  
    
  
  The focused wave in the 2D numerical wave tank, computed with code_saturne (run a023, the same run as
  the results below). Propagation at real speed, then breaking in 4x slow motion. Full tank above, breaking zone
  below; water coloured by speed, air in grey, arrows show the water velocity.

Assessing the loads on offshore wind turbines starts with getting the wave itself right, from the wave-maker to the moment it overturns. This case reproduces, in 2D, the wave validation of the following paper. Its subject is a focused, extreme breaking wave from the DIMPACT experiments (wave 7: Hs = 0.13 m, Tp = 2.49 s).






NoteDeep water focused breaking wave loads on a fixed cylinder



Batlle Martin, M., Harris, J. C., Filipot, J.-F., Hulin, F., Tassin, A. and Renaud, P. (2023). Coastal Engineering 186, 104397.
Read the paper   doi:10.1016/j.coastaleng.2023.104397





The 2D numerical wave tank. Ifremer’s flume has a piston wave-maker at x = 0. The models start at x = 2 m from velocities computed by a potential-flow (BEM) simulation of the paddle motion. They focus the wave near x = 20 m and absorb it downstream.


The wave is computed with two CFD codes:

code_saturne 7.0.5 is the code of the paper, developed by EDF (code-saturne.org; Archambeau et al., 2004). It tracks the free surface with an algebraic volume-of-fluid (VOF) method.
OpenFOAM® v2406 (openfoam.com; Weller et al., 1998) runs the fluxinator solver. It reconstructs the free surface geometrically with isoAdvector (Roenby et al., 2016) and PLIC-RDF (Scheufler and Roenby, 2019).

Everything else is identical in the two codes: the same mesh of 47,004 cells (25 mm cells at the free surface), the same measured inlet velocities with their spikes removed, the same outlet damping zone and the same wave gauges. Both run on a desktop PC with 6 cores, in 5.1 h (code_saturne) and 1.2 h (OpenFOAM).

title: Numerical wave tank: focused wave
text:
Results at a glance

Temporal evaluation



Free-surface elevation at the last wave gauge before breaking: experiment (open circles), code_saturne (blue) and OpenFOAM (red).


Both codes follow the measured wave record closely. At this gauge, the RMS error over t = 10-26 s is 1.9 mm for code_saturne and 2.4 mm for OpenFOAM. The highest crest (232 mm measured) is within 1 mm in code_saturne and 3 mm too high in OpenFOAM, and both arrive within 4 ms of the measurement. Model time is shifted by 6 ms, because the flume’s paddle lagged its command by 6 ms, and the model gauges are read at the real probe positions.


Spatial evaluation



Free-surface profiles during overturning at t = 29.4, 29.6 and 29.8 s: experiment from the camera (open circles), code_saturne (blue) and OpenFOAM (red).


Both codes reproduce the shape of the steep front recorded by the camera. The code_saturne front is 2-3 cm behind the camera and the OpenFOAM front 4-6 cm behind, one to two mesh cells. This is within the uncertainty of the camera profiles themselves: two ways of processing the same video differ by about 4 cm.

title: About me
text:
I am Marc Batlle Martin, a civil engineer and fluid dynamicist from Torroella de Montgrí. My work is about making numerical models useful to engineers, scientists and policymakers.
I am currently working at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center.
